extracted.intended_audience: general public and fans of comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarises the demonstrable principles, techniques, and production choices that characterise John Cleese's comedy as described on his Wikipedia page. Focuses on stylistic, structural, and pragmatic criteria that one could use to analyse or emulate his work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialisation in genres
rubrics_metrics.description: Cleese has specialised in political and religious satire, black comedy, sketch comedy, and surreal humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly listed on the page; examples include Monty Python sketches and Fawlty Towers. Use this as a taxonomy when evaluating whether a piece is 'in Cleese's wheelhouse' — i.e., does it use satire, black humour, sketch structure, or surrealism?

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary situations turned absurd
rubrics_metrics.description: Their humour often involved ordinary people in ordinary situations behaving absurdly for no obvious reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This recurring device (page quote) is exemplified by sketches such as the Dead Parrot and Cheese Shop. When producing or judging material, check whether the piece grounds itself in the familiar before escalating into absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of authority figures as targets/vehicles
rubrics_metrics.description: Their sketches often involved authority figures (policemen, detectives, Nazi officers, government officials) which Cleese then proceeded to undermine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cleese's comic persona often takes the form of a pompous or official figure whose self-importance is exposed and satirised (e.g., Ministry of Silly Walks). Evaluate how effectively the piece juxtaposes authority and ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadpan / poker-face delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Cleese's 'poker face', clipped middle class accent, and stone-faced delivery are key performance tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page cites 'poker face' and instances such as Argument Clinic. Assessors should note timing, restraint, and straight-man technique: the funnier the absurdity, often the straighter the delivery required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highly articulate argument about arbitrary subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Sketches where two characters conduct 'highly articulate arguments over completely arbitrary subjects' (e.g., Argument Clinic, Cheese Shop).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a specific comedic device: rigorous, formal language applied to trivial or nonsensical topics. When writing or evaluating, look for precision of language used for inherently silly content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surreal twist elevates mundane premise
rubrics_metrics.description: Transforming a mundane complaint/premise into a surreal element (example: 'Dead Parrot' — originally a toaster or broken car; Chapman suggested changing it to a 'dead parrot' giving the sketch a surreal air).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page highlights the creative decision that made the sketch memorable. Criterion for quality: did a single surreal change meaningfully elevate the material?

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical exaggeration / grotesque physicality
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of exaggerated physical actions to satirise (e.g., Ministry of Silly Walks: a 'grotesquely elaborate walk'), where physicality embodies the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate economy and inventiveness of physical business; does the movement encapsulate and amplify the satirical target (bureaucracy, pomposity)?

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic contrast / foil dynamic
rubrics_metrics.description: The recurring Cleese–Palin dynamic: Cleese's crazed aggression contrasted with Palin's shuffling inoffensiveness, used as a comic foil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure how pairings exploit physical and vocal contrast to heighten humour. Good use of foil clarifies character roles and amplifies comedic beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire used to discredit objectionable views
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of ridicule as a means to discredit reactionary or prejudiced views (example cited: laughing at Alf Garnett to 'discredit' his views).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging satirical intent and effect, consider whether the humour targets and undermines the objectionable stance rather than endorsing it; context and framing are key (page discussion of Fawlty Towers and Alf Garnett).

rubrics_metrics.name: Context matters for offensiveness / creative freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Cleese's stated view: 'The main thing is to realise that words depend on their context [...] PC people simply don't understand this business about context because they tend to be very literal-minded', and that PC/'wokeism' can 'stifle creativity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit stance about boundaries in humour. Use it as a criterion when debating acceptability: assessors should weigh context and satirical intent, not only literal content, though this remains contested in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Straight-man performance to highlight absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: Performing the straight bureaucrat/stony-faced role (e.g., Cleese in Argument Clinic) to make trivial bickering or nonsense more absurd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate timing, restraint, and precision: the straight delivery must be credible enough to contrast with the absurd, thereby creating humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of real-life inspiration for characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawing on real people and experiences when creating characters (e.g., Basil Fawlty based on Donald Sinclair).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether observational detail and specificity derived from real-life sources make characters more vivid and recognisable; note ethical considerations about representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control scope/length to preserve quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Production choice: Fawlty Towers consisted of two seasons, each of only six episodes; Cleese and Booth stated this was 'to avoid compromising the quality of the series.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a production guideline, favour brevity and selectivity rather than quantity when aiming for consistently high-quality comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reworking and repurposing material across mediums
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples show material evolving across radio, TV, stage and film (e.g., sketches appearing in different forms such as pre-Python specials, Flying Circus, and films).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for effectiveness: does the piece adapt well to different media while preserving its core comedic logic? Look for successful escalation or transposition of a sketch into film or stage.
